items.a: It depends on what the site needs, but Squarespace's entry plan does more for the same price. Both cheapest paid plans cost $25 a month: Webflow's Basic has no CMS, so a site with a blog needs Premium at $39 a month instead, while Squarespace's $25 Basic plan already includes a blog, an online store and invoicing. The gap widens with traffic, not just features. Every Squarespace plan includes unlimited bandwidth, so a busy site's bill never moves for that reason. Webflow's Premium plan includes only 50 GB of bandwidth a month, and a site that outgrows it needs a separate, metered bandwidth add-on on top of the plan price, which is usually what pushes a real Webflow bill well past its $39 sticker price. Team size adds a similar gap: Webflow charges $19 a month for every editor beyond the owner, while Squarespace's Core plan and up include unlimited contributors for one flat $39 fee.

items.q: Which is easier to use, Webflow or Squarespace?
items.a: Squarespace, for most people with no design background. Its editor works with pre-built sections and blocks: pick a template, swap in text and images, and the layout stays consistent without writing any code. Webflow is built the opposite way: its visual canvas gives near-code-level control over layout and custom code, and that same control is what takes real time to learn, which is why it suits designers and technically comfortable owners more than someone who wants a guided template. Neither tool requires hiring a developer for a standard site, and Webflow's free Starter plan lets you practice on its builder for as long as you like before publishing anywhere. The practical way to decide is by what the site needs: a straightforward business site with a blog or a store fits Squarespace's guided approach well, while a site that needs a specific, custom look is worth the time it takes to learn Webflow's builder instead.

items.q: Can I move my site from Squarespace to Webflow, or the other way, later?
items.a: Expect to rebuild, not just move a file, in either direction. Both are hosted, proprietary platforms rather than something you run yourself, so a site's design and checkout only exist inside the platform that built them. Webflow does publish a documented export path: a paid Workspace plan can export a site's HTML and CSS, and CMS content exports one Collection at a time, though forms and any server-side features stop working once you leave. Squarespace's help center, in the pages checked for this record, does not describe an equivalent site or code export option, so moving a Squarespace site elsewhere in practice means rebuilding the design and re-entering content by hand. Neither platform's billing locks you into a long-term contract by default: both run month to month unless you choose annual billing, and switching between them only changes the term you're paying for, not a multi-year commitment. Budget real time for a full move either way, not a quick import.

items.q: Does Squarespace charge per team member the way Webflow does?
items.a: No, not above its entry plan — a real structural difference between the two. Squarespace's Basic plan caps a site at 2 contributors, including the owner, but Core, Plus and Advanced include unlimited contributors for one flat plan price, with no extra fee no matter how many people log in. Webflow works the opposite way: the owner's seat is free on every Workspace, but every additional editor needs a paid seat, $19 a month for a Limited seat that edits content, or $45 a month for a Full seat with design access, and that fee applies whether the Workspace is free or paid. A team of two stays on Squarespace's $25 Basic plan, since Basic's cap is 2 contributors including the owner; a third editor is what forces the move to Core, at $39 a month. At that same size, Webflow's Starter Workspace plus two $19 Limited seats ($38 total) narrowly undercuts Core. Past that, Squarespace's flat pricing wins outright: a team of eight pays the same $39 Core plan a third person would, while Webflow's per-seat fee keeps adding up with every hire.

items.q: Why does Webflow charge for bandwidth when Squarespace doesn't?
items.a: Because the two price hosting differently, and it is one of the clearest catches in Webflow's pricing. Webflow's Premium plan, $39 a month, includes only 50 GB of bandwidth; past that, the site needs a separate, metered add-on, and Webflow only publishes a page-view range rather than a fixed per-visit figure, so predicting the right tier is an estimate, not a guarantee. A site that goes over its limit for two consecutive months gets bumped to a higher, non-refundable tier automatically, though the first month over is not charged. Squarespace made a different choice: every current plan, Basic through Advanced, includes unlimited bandwidth, so a traffic spike or a steady rise in visitors never triggers an extra charge or a forced upgrade. That matters most for a site expecting real growth: budget for Webflow's bandwidth add-on ahead of time rather than treating a surprise upgrade as a billing error, or pick the plan where bandwidth is simply not metered.

items.q: Which is better for selling online courses or digital downloads?
items.a: Squarespace, on paper, has the more direct fit. It prices digital-content and membership sales on their own fee ladder, separate from its online-store fee, stepping down from 7% on Basic to 0% on Advanced, $139 a month, as the plan price rises. Webflow's published plans don't list an equivalent fee tier for digital downloads or memberships; its Ecommerce plans are built around a shipped product catalog, with item caps from 500 to 15,000 and a 2% fee on the entry tier only. Neither platform, though, is a dedicated course platform: there is no cohort scheduling, drip-fed lessons or built-in community feature documented on either one. A creator selling a handful of downloads or a self-paced video course can use either tool's commerce features well enough, with Squarespace's fee structure the more transparent of the two, but one who needs real course infrastructure should look at a platform built specifically for that instead.
